newsitem.title: USA: U.S. concerned at threat to Cambodian elections.
newsitem.headline: U.S. concerned at threat to Cambodian elections.

text.p: The United States said on Wednesday that political violence in Cambodia could threaten the country's capacity to stage free and fair elections next year.

The State Department said Deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott expressed the U.S. concerns at a meeting with Cambodian opposition leader Sam Rainsy, apparent target of a March 30 grenade attack on a demonstration he was leading.

Rainsy narrowly escaped injury from blasts that left up to 19 people dead and more than 100 injured in Phnom Penh. The United States has condemned the attack and urged the Cambodian government to find and punish the culprits.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said Talbott told Rainsy of U.S. "concern about the impact of political violence on Cambodia's ability to hold free and fair elections in 1998."

"We are deeply concerned that acts of violence such as this could put at risk the significant progress toward democracy that Cambodia has made since the U.N.-sponsored elections in 1993," Burns told a news briefing.

Burns said that "as a friend", the United States had been telling Cambodia's leaders of its concern over recent cases of threats to freedom of expression and the press, and how such trends could jeopardise international support for Cambodia.

Following the grenade attack, Cambodia's Interior Ministry Wednesday slapped a temporary ban on street protests, in a move condemned as unconstitutional by human rights groups and Rainsy's Khmer Nation Party.

The ministry has launched an investigation into the attack outside parliament, but many people, including First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh, have expressed doubts it would bring those responsible to justice.
